1:
Delitzsch sets the chapter in its place before reading a word of it. The temple was the great work of the reign, and beside it everything else falls into the background, so that both histories enumerate the rest only summarily; he then divides this chapter into its four notices, the cities, the statute labour, the sacrificial service, and the voyage to Ophir. On the twenty years Clarke does the arithmetic, seven years and a half for the temple and twelve and a half or thirteen for his own house, and Ellicott reckons the same span from the fourth year of the reign.

The cities Huram had restored are the hard place, and Ellicott spends his longest note on them. Kings says the opposite of what stands here: there Solomon gives Huram twenty cities in Galilee, which do not please him, so that they get a name meaning like-nought. Three explanations are on offer. Josephus says Huram returned the despised cities and Solomon then repaired and peopled them, which is what the English version here assumes; others suppose an exchange of friendly gifts, twenty Israelite cities one way and twenty from the coast the other, which Ellicott calls highly improbable; and Ellicott's own reading is that the chronicler passed over a fact that seemed to lessen Solomon, the surrender of the territory, and chose to speak of Huram's non-acceptance as a gift. He then defends the result squarely: this is neither an effacement nor a travesty, as Reuss has it, nor even a remodelling in Solomon's favour, but another statement equally true and not incompatible with the older one. Delitzsch presses the same point from the verb, which here means not fortifying but completing, since the cities were in very bad condition; and he reads the following clause as Solomon transplanting Israelites into them, the border being chiefly inhabited by Gentiles. Gill reports the transaction flatly, that Solomon gave them first and Huram, not liking them, gave them back.

The march on Hamath-zobah is the one military act in the reign, and Gill says so: this is the only instance of any warlike expedition of Solomon's, against Coelesyria, which David had subdued and which had perhaps rebelled. Ellicott notes that the conquest of Hamath, a kingdom on friendly terms with David, is recorded neither in Kings nor anywhere else in the Old Testament, and he adopts Thenius's reduction of it, that what is described is not the taking of Hamath itself but the annexation of part of its territory in the fruitful plain to its south. Delitzsch settles only the name, that Hamath-zobah is not the city Hamath lying in Zobah.

On the building list the commentators divide identification from purpose. Tadmor is Palmyra, as Clarke says in a line and Ellicott at length, set on the traders' route between the coast and Thapsacus on the Euphrates; that Solomon founded the place, Ellicott adds, is still the tradition of the country. The store cities in Hamath he takes for places of arms, outposts against the neighbouring kingdom and victualling stations, and he observes that the description of Beth-horon's walls and gates and bars is wanting in Kings, while Baalath, a Danite town west of Jerusalem, served as a bulwark against the Philistines. He closes by noting what is missing: nothing here of the fortifying of Jerusalem, or of Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer, which Pharaoh had taken and given to his daughter. Henry reads the same list for character rather than geography, that a man of Solomon's learning spent his days not in his study but in his country, that it is the interest of a state to promote industry and keep its subjects from idleness, and that Solomon knew how to set bounds to his desires, finishing all he desired to build and then desiring no more, unlike Alexander fretting that he had no more worlds to conquer.
8:
The levy fell on the children of the peoples Israel had not consumed, and not on Israelites, who appear instead as men of war and captains; and on that list Delitzsch makes two corrections. He would reorder the words to match the parallel in Kings, and he insists on the sense of one of the titles: these are not chariot combatants but royal adjutants, and he sends the reader to the places where the word is used of the officers of Pharaoh and of David. The overseers are the harder problem, since this text counts two hundred and fifty of them where Kings has five hundred and fifty. Delitzsch resolves it by nationality rather than by emendation: the two hundred and fifty here were Israelites, while the larger figure takes in the chief overseers of both nations. On the spelling of their title he holds that the consonantal text is right and that the marginal reading has come in from the other history. Clarke passes the whole section by with a cross-reference.

Then the Egyptian princess is moved out of the city of David, and the notice is awkward where it stands. Delitzsch says why it stands here at all: it belongs to the history of Solomon's buildings, which is the thread being followed, and it comes in abruptly only because this writer never mentioned the marriage in the first place. Ellicott adds what little can be said about her, that she was probably of the dynasty founded by Shishak, which was of Semitic origin, and that the chronicler brings her in here solely in connection with the buildings. On the reason given for the removal he makes two observations: the motive is wanting in the other text and is characteristic of this writer in both thought and language, and the title king of Israel is set against her Egyptian origin. He will not go as far as Thenius, who held that she could have lived nowhere but in the old palace of David until the new one was finished; the older account says only that Solomon brought her into the city of David.

What the removal shows about Solomon divides the rest. Clarke takes it as evidence in his favour, asking whether this is not proof that he considered his wife a heathen and unfit to dwell in a place that had been sanctified, and concluding that Solomon had not yet departed from the true God; he also passes on a later tradition that names her Bithiah. Wesley puts it as a matter of precaution, that the ark was then in the house of David, which therefore ought to be kept pure and free from the very danger and appearance of pollution. Henry works the contrast harder than either. The house of David had been a place of great piety, where the ark had stood and where holy David had prayed many a good prayer and sung many a sweet psalm, and her house was perhaps a place of great vanity; she had likely been proselyted, but it is a question whether all her servants were, and they may have had among them the idols of Egypt. Henry grants that Solomon had not zeal and courage enough to suppress and punish what was amiss there, and credits him only with consulting the honour of his father's memory. He then guards the argument against proving too much: it is not that every place the ark had rested in became holy, for then the houses of Abinadab and Obed-edom must have been so too, but that this place had held it long and publicly. The principle he draws is his own: between things sacred and things common the ancient landmarks ought to be kept up.
12:
The opening word is read the same way by everyone: after the consecration. Ellicott and Delitzsch both add that the sacrifices are now offered on the altar Solomon built and apparently no longer at Gibeon, where he had sacrificed at the beginning of the reign, and Ellicott notes that the detail of its standing before the porch is absent from Kings. Both also mark the difference of scale, Kings recording only that Solomon sacrificed three times a year where this account is detailed. On the frequency Gill and Ellicott agree against a narrow reading: Gill says the verse does not mean barely at the time of the rebuilding of the cities, for it was his constant practice, and Ellicott that he offered not once but habitually. Delitzsch gives the daily rate a close grammatical reading, taking the clause about the commandment of Moses as an explanatory subordinate clause interpolated into the main sentence; Ellicott renders the same phrase literally as with a day's matter on a day, and observes that the plural form used for the set seasons occurs nowhere else.

On the courses the accounts converge. Gill supplies the number, the twenty-four courses that served weekly in their turns; Ellicott glosses the verb as caused to stand and the Levites' charges as watches, wards and stations; Delitzsch runs the whole arrangement back to the institutions of David, the classes of priests, the Levites at their stations, the doorkeepers by their courses. The title given David draws comment twice. Wesley takes the man of God to mean a prophet inspired by God in these matters, so that his commands are therefore the commands of God. Henry notices that the title is the one given to Moses, and for the same reason, that David was both instructed and authorised of God to make these establishments; and he draws the lesson from Solomon's restraint, that though he was the builder of the temple he did not attempt to amend, alter or add to what the man of God had commanded in God's name, but closely adhered to it and used his own authority to see it observed. Henry puts the result as a sequence: he observed God's laws, and then all obeyed his orders.

Whose commandment it was that none departed from is the one point of real division. Clarke answers in five words, that it was the institutions of David, and Ellicott agrees that the king here is David, while Gill reads it the other way, that the priests and Levites departed not from the commandment of Solomon, which was itself according to the order of David. Ellicott also wants the text mended, holding that the preposition meaning from has fallen out of the Hebrew and must be restored on the authority of three manuscripts and the versions. Delitzsch declines the emendation, since the verb is construed here with the accusative in the sense of transgressing a command, so that no alteration is necessary.

The closing verse divides again, over what was prepared and until when. Gill and Wesley read it of the materials: everything was procured and the very stones and timber made fit beforehand, so that nothing retarded the completion. Ellicott reads the word as completed, a late usage, and sees Solomon's activity divided into two periods, the preparations up to the foundation and then the prosecution of the work to its end; but he reports that all the versions take the phrase the other way, from the day of the foundation to the completion, and allows that this writer's Hebrew may well use it for the starting point. Delitzsch fixes the day differently again, as the day on which the regular worship began, immediately after the dedication. Henry is content to say what the perfecting consisted in: the work was the main matter, not the place, and the temple was unfinished till all this was done.
17:
Whether Solomon went down to the coast himself is the first disagreement, and it turns on how much weight the verb will bear. Henry takes the journey literally and draws a maxim from it, that he did himself in person visit the sea-port towns, since those who deal much in the world will find it their interest so far as they can to inspect their affairs themselves and to see with their own eyes. Ellicott denies the inference: the words of this text do not necessarily imply a personal visit, and what Solomon did was to send his shipwrights down to the port in Edom. Gill supplies only the occasion, that the king was now at leisure to look after his navy and carry on his merchandise. On the place-name Ellicott collects the variations, one version making Ezion-geber a city over against Eloth where Kings has it near Eloth, and the plain sea of this text standing for the Red Sea of Kings and of the Vulgate. Delitzsch dates the voyage from the same opening word, placing it after the building of the temple and the palace, in the second half of the reign, and settles the destination against the commoner guess: Ophir is not to be sought in India but in southern Arabia. Clarke leaves both the port and Ophir to conjecture.

How the ships reached the gulf is Ellicott's set piece, and he works it as a dilemma that dissolves. The vessels were a gift from the Tyrian ally once Solomon began to show an interest in maritime affairs, but the text does not say to what port they were sent. If they were sent to Ezion-geber, then either they were dragged across the desert that divides the Mediterranean from the gulf, or they sailed round Africa; and Ellicott is willing to grant that neither is impossible, since the Greek historians of later times often speak of the transport of ships overland and the galleys of that age were probably small, while the circumnavigation of Africa was in fact achieved by an expedition sent out by Necho some four centuries afterwards. His own solution needs neither. If the Tyrian king supplied skilled mariners, they would naturally sail in their own ships no further than Joppa; the ships could be left there while a part of their crews went on overland to Ezion-geber by Solomon's order. The phrase ships and servants, he concludes, means ships with servants, or ships conveying them, and the men who made the voyage were the Tyrian king's.

Clarke reaches the same division of labour from the other end, by the character of the two peoples. Solomon probably bore the expenses while his friend furnished the expert sailors, for the Jews at no period of their history had any skill in maritime affairs, their navigation being confined to the lakes of their own country, from which no nautical skill could be acquired; the Tyrians, on the contrary, lived on and in the sea.

The figure brought home is the one place where the two histories plainly differ, four hundred and fifty talents here against four hundred and twenty there, and Ellicott accounts for it as a copyist's slip, two Hebrew letters having been confused. Henry does not touch the arithmetic but reads the whole enterprise as a lesson in dependence. Canaan was a rich country and yet had to send to Ophir for gold; the Israelites were a wise and understanding people and yet had to be beholden to the king of Tyre for men who had knowledge of the seas. And this although Canaan was God's peculiar land and Israel his peculiar people, which teaches, Henry says, that grace and not gold is the best riches, and acquaintance with God and his law, rather than with arts and sciences, the best knowledge.
